articles.title: A family of eight bought a $1.41 million Nantucket cottage expecting to expand its two bedrooms, but a deed restriction banned additions; a jury and judge awarded nearly $1.3 million against the broker
articles.summary: Squeezing eight family members into a 1,200-square-foot cottage sounds like the setup for a cramped summer sitcom, yet for a Connecticut couple, that
articles.body: Squeezing eight family members into a 1,200-square-foot cottage sounds like the setup for a cramped summer sitcom, yet for a Connecticut couple, that coastal squeeze turned into a five-year courtroom drama. Hoping to carve out a spacious retreat on one of America’s priciest islands, Dr. Mary Murray and attorney Jeffrey Ment bought a modest Nantucket house on the promise that they could double its footprint, only to discover too late that legal restrictions froze the home’s size permanently.Promises of expansion on Polpis RoadAccording to Realtor, Murray, an obstetrician, and Ment, a lawyer, reside in Westport, Connecticut, and regularly vacationed on Nantucket with their six children. After previously relying on William Raveis Nantucket agent Melanie Gowen to secure island rentals, the couple worked with her in 2020 to purchase a two-bedroom cottage at 151 Polpis Road for $1.41 million, though Nantucket Current noted the sale price at $1.45 million. With Nantucket’s median listing price hovering near $6 million, the buyers viewed the property as a rare foothold in an ultracompetitive market, Realtor report added.Because a two-bedroom layout could not accommodate a family of eight, Murray and Ment sought assurances before closing. Gowen, who also presented herself as possessing interior design and property development experience on the island, allegedly informed the buyers that she had visited the local building department and confirmed the undersized structure could be doubled in size, Realtor report noted. She even sketched out a potential addition, shared a video of the planned build, and suggested in writing that local bedroom limits could be bypassed by labeling new rooms as dens or living spaces, according to Realtor.A deed restriction halts plans and sparks a lawsuitWhen the couple contacted town officials in early 2021 regarding septic upgrades and construction, they learned that zoning rules and a strict deed restriction prohibited adding even a single square foot to the house, according to both outlets. After Gowen’s colleague Kenny Hilbig confirmed the deed restriction and unsuccessful attempts were made to arrange a property trade or a brokerage bridge loan, representatives indicated the couple would need to file suit to recover losses from the firm directly, Realtor reported.In June 2021, Murray and Ment filed an action in Norfolk Superior Court alleging negligence, breach of fiduciary duty, misrepresentation, and violations of the Massachusetts Consumer Protection Act, known as Chapter 93A, Realtor noted. Following a multi-year legal battle, a jury ruled in the buyers’ favor in January 2026, awarding $1,280,886 in damages—a figure that included over $867,000 in doubled damages alongside interest and legal expenses, Nantucket Current reported. The jury attributed 65 percent of the negligence to Gowen and 35 percent to the buyers, according to Nantucket Current. Superior Court Judge Ira Gant upheld the verdict and issued an amended judgment in June 2026, both outlets noted.Defense arguments and the financial falloutWilliam Raveis Nantucket and Gowen have denied wrongdoing and filed a notice of appeal in October 2026, while interest continues accruing on the nearly $1.3 million judgment, Nantucket Current reported. In statements to both outlets, brokerage attorney Ray Cashen—also spelled Chasen by Nantucket Current—argued that Ment admitted during trial testimony he did not believe Gowen intentionally lied. Defense counsel further contended that the buyers received the restrictive document eleven days before closing, had two attorneys review it, unsuccessfully asked the sellers to waive a two-bedroom septic restriction, and still completed the purchase, Realtor reported. Brokerage representatives also maintained to Nantucket Current that the firm upholds high standards of integrity across its decades-long history.Ultimately, Murray and Ment sold the Polpis Road cottage in 2021 for $1.95 million, though Murray told Nantucket Current that mortgage payments, improvements, and Land Bank fees reduced their net gain to roughly $125,000. Forced back into a surging market where entry-level properties had climbed past $2 million, the couple borrowed against their retirement accounts and took out a home equity loan to purchase a five-bedroom home on Gardener Road for $3.1 million, leaving them carrying substantial debt despite their courtroom victory, according to both outlets.Image Courtesy: Google GeminiYou use AI every day. articles.title: A Vermont woman’s neighbour repeatedly parked his truck so close to her car that she had to crawl through the passenger door to reach the driver's seat; the Supreme Court ruled in her favour, upholding a $15,000 nuisance award against him
articles.summary: A Vermont woman who repeatedly found herself unable to get in or out of her car because of her neighbour's parking, has won a legal battle after the
articles.body: A Vermont woman who repeatedly found herself unable to get in or out of her car because of her neighbour's parking, has won a legal battle after the state's Supreme Court upheld a $15,000 nuisance award against him. The dispute involved a shared gravel driveway, where the neighbour allegedly positioned his truck so close to her vehicle that she sometimes had to climb through the passenger door to reach the driver's seat. The case also involved allegations of snow being dumped onto her property and other deliberate acts of interference.Vermont Supreme Court upholds $15,000 award over the driveway disputeThe case concerned Misty McCartney, who owns a property next to a rental property belonging to David Burns and Melissa Haberman. Their neighbouring properties share a gravel driveway, which became the centre of a prolonged disagreement over parking arrangements and access rights.In its January 9, 2026 decision, the Vermont Supreme Court rejected the neighbours' appeal and upheld the lower court's findings in McCartney's favour. The decision followed a civil case in which the Vermont Superior Court had awarded her $15,000 for the inconvenience, discomfort and distress caused by what it found to be a continuing private nuisance.How the shared driveway became a source of conflictThe disagreement dates back to 2019, when McCartney purchased her property from a previous owner. Burns and Haberman owned the neighbouring rental property but lived elsewhere. The two properties were connected by a gravel driveway that had been used by both sides for years.The arrangement was complicated by the property's history. According to the Vermont Superior Court's June 2025 findings in McCartney v Burns, the driveway was substantially located on McCartney's land, although approximately 3 feet of its width extended onto the neighbouring property.The court traced the right-of-way back to 1905, when an earlier owner reserved access across part of the land. A 1974 deed later referred to a 20-foot-wide right-of-way, but its description contained mistakes about the property boundaries and the location of the neighbouring houses.These differences became important when Burns wanted tenants at the rental property to park in the shared driveway. McCartney maintained that the right-of-way was intended for access rather than parking and referred to a property survey to support her position.What did the neighbour allegedly do to make parking difficultThe Superior Court found that Burns began deliberately positioning his vehicle to interfere with McCartney's ability to use the driveway after she challenged his interpretation of the parking arrangements.The behaviour reportedly continued over months and years. On some occasions, Burns waited until McCartney had parked her car and gone inside before moving his truck close to it. The positioning made it extremely difficult for her to leave the property or even get into the driver's seat.The court recorded incidents in which she had to crawl through the passenger door to reach the steering wheel. At other times, Burns allegedly positioned his truck before she returned home, leaving her with little room to manoeuvre through the driveway.The dispute also extended beyond parking. During snowfall, Burns deliberately moved snow from the rental property into piles along the shared driveway and onto McCartney's land, according to the court's findings. She eventually arranged for part of her front yard to be ploughed so she could park somewhere her neighbour could not block her vehicle.The Superior Court also documented other incidents, including Burns leaving a pile of animal waste near her back steps and refusing an offer to move a metal cabinet from her barn. The cabinet was instead left near the property boundary and later fell over, damaging a vehicle.The dispute also affected her personal life and workMcCartney became increasingly fearful of going outside because she expected further confrontations. The court described her as hypervigilant and noted that she had difficulty sleeping. Her mother also observed changes in her mood, while the dispute affected her relationship with her then-boyfriend.Her work was affected as well. On some days, she could not leave home because her vehicle had been blocked in by Burns's truck. The judge acknowledged that the conduct did not meet the legal threshold for intentional infliction of emotional distress. However, that did not mean the behaviour was too minor to justify a nuisance claim.The court decided that the conduct amounted to a sustained campaign to cause annoyance and inconvenience.How did the courts settle the driveway rightsIn its June 2025 order, the Superior Court clarified how the shared driveway could be used. It determined that the right-of-way should be 15 feet wide, with the actual gravel driveway limited to 8 feet. The right-of-way was to pass equally across the two properties for the first 58.86 feet.The court also established parking restrictions. Neither party could park within the eight-foot gravel driveway or obstruct snow removal and other maintenance work. Additional rules required the neighbours to avoid parking within the right-of-way when the local weather forecast predicted at least two inches of snow over the following 12 hours.On the financial side, McCartney received $950 for physical damage to her vehicles and another $50 in nominal damages for individual trespasses. The separate nuisance award amounted to $15,000, bringing the damages awarded across the claims to $16,000.The judge also issued a permanent injunction covering both Burns and Haberman, aimed at preventing further violations of McCartney's property rights.Why did the Vermont Supreme Court uphold the decisionBurns and Haberman challenged the lower court's interpretation of the shared driveway and the way it had corrected the wording of the 1974 deed.They argued that the right-of-way should have been located entirely on McCartney's property rather than divided between the two neighbouring properties. They also disputed the lower court's interpretation of the earlier deeds and the history of the access arrangement.However, in its January 9, 2026 ruling, the Vermont Supreme Court found no reason to overturn the decision. The appeal was dismissed and the lower court's decision was affirmed.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Jeff Bridges is fronting a new US child-hunger campaign announced on November 16, with $5 million in planned grants and a goal of connecting 10 million more children to reliable meals by 2032
articles.summary: Jeff Bridges is fronting a new national child hunger campaign launched by No Kid Hungry on November 16, according to PR Newswire.
articles.body: Jeff Bridges is fronting a new national child hunger campaign launched by No Kid Hungry on November 16, according to PR Newswire. The initiative, called Amplify Impact, aims to connect 10 million more children to reliable meals by 2032, beginning with $5 million in planned grants and a nationwide advertising campaign featuring the Academy Award winning actor.The campaign comes at a time when rising costs continue to strain family budgets and one in five children in America faces hunger. No Kid Hungry says it wants to build on programmes that already work, strengthen local nutrition systems, and help families access food in a way that feels simple, dignified, and predictable. Read more about the initiative, as per the release, here:A campaign with a clear goalAmplify Impact is a nationwide effort running through 2027, with the long term aim of reaching 10 million more children by 2032. No Kid Hungry says it will raise an additional $150 million on top of existing fundraising to support that goal.The campaign will focus on partnerships, programmes, and policy solutions. Rather than treating hunger as a problem that can be solved through one type of intervention, the organisation wants to connect school meals, food assistance, and community based nutrition support.Anne Filipic, chief executive of Share Our Strength, the organisation behind No Kid Hungry, said in the release that the goal is to build a safety net that works around how families actually live. She argued that children should be able to count on three meals a day, every day.Jeff Bridges fronting the messageBridges, who has served as a national spokesperson for No Kid Hungry, will appear in the campaign’s advertising. The campaign will spotlight communities across the country that are developing practical solutions to childhood hunger.The featured locations include New Orleans, Miami, Los Angeles, Chicago, Washington DC and Virginia, and Texas. By showing how local programmes are working, the campaign aims to make the issue feel less abstract and more connected to real families.Bridges’ involvement brings recognisable attention to a problem that often remains hidden. His role is not just to lend a famous face, but to help communicate the urgency of making sure children have consistent access to food.A $5 million investmentTo mark the launch, No Kid Hungry is investing an additional $5 million in partners working to strengthen and scale nutrition programmes. The grants are intended to support organisations that can help expand access to meals and improve the systems families rely on.The organisation says the money will help partners reimagine the food system so it better meets the needs of families. That includes making programmes easier to use and ensuring that support reaches children before hunger becomes a crisis.Filipic said the organisation cannot reach 10 million more children alone. She argued that the programmes and policies that feed children were built through collaboration and will need the same approach to be protected and expanded.A New York launch eventThe campaign kicked off with a Give Back Bodega pop up at 873 Broadway in New York City. The two day event, running November 18 and 19, transformed a neighbourhood bodega into a space focused on community and food access.Top Chef winner Danny Garcia created his own version of a classic New York bodega breakfast sandwich for the event. Visitors could enjoy the food while making optional donations to support the fight against childhood hunger.Special guests included Summer House star Lindsay Hubbard and chef Lorena Garcia, who helped serve sandwiches and raise awareness. The event was designed to capture the comfort of a neighbourhood bodega while reminding people that not every child can count on having enough to eat.Measuring what worksAmplify Impact will also introduce a vision for the No Kid Hungry Index. This future facing tool is intended to show how effectively existing programmes are meeting children’s food needs and identify where support can be strengthened.A seven state prototype is planned for 2027, with the goal of eventually expanding to all 50 states. The idea is to give communities and policymakers a clearer picture of what is working and where gaps remain.By combining grants, advertising, local partnerships, and data, the campaign hopes to create lasting change rather than short term relief. The focus is on building a system that families can rely on over time.Why this matters nowChild hunger remains a persistent issue in the United States, particularly as food costs continue to rise. No Kid Hungry says millions of children live with hunger, and that uncertainty around meals can affect health, learning, and family stability.The organisation’s approach is built around the belief that this problem can be solved. By investing in programmes that already work and pushing for stronger systems, it hopes to make reliable meals a normal part of childhood rather than an exception.With Bridges fronting the campaign and $5 million in grants already planned, Amplify Impact begins with both visibility and practical support. The real test will be whether the effort can turn its ambitious 2032 goal into lasting access to food for millions of children.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Trump holds the nuclear cards to play against China and Russia on arms control
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's arms control push meets a China arsenal that doubled from 300 warheads in 2020 to over 600, as New START expired Feb. 5.
articles.body: Nuclear weapons aren’t usually a topic at APEC, but trilateral arms control has been on the mind of President Donald J. Trump since at least last spring. And after launching Operation Epic Fury to end Iran’s path to a nuclear weapon, no one can doubt Trump is serious about the nuclear menace. What better moment than this historic trilateral meeting between Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin? Turns out China is also a growing nuclear problem. Driven by Xi Jinping’s ambitions, China has doubled its arsenal from 300 nuclear warheads in 2020 to over 600 today. American policymakers have little visibility into China’s intentions. And of course, the last nuclear arms control treaty with Russia, called New START, expired on Feb. 5. TRUMP KICKS OFF HIGH-STAKES ASIA TRIP WITH XI, PUTIN MEETINGS LOOMING ON WORLD STAGE Trump raised trilateral arms control during his May trip to Beijing, and again during Xi’s visit to Washington. "The President advocated for trilateral arms control negotiations" among the three countries, the White House statement said on Sept. 24. No U.S. president has ever tried to coax China into nuclear arms control. It’s a monumental task, but perhaps the moment is now. THREE MANILA MOMENTS THAT GIVE TRUMP MOMENTUM GOING INTO TALKS WITH CHINA The Pentagon estimates China’s arsenal will reach 1,000 warheads by 2030 and continue to 1,500. Last year, China paraded its new JL-3 submarine-launched ballistic missile with a range of 5,400 miles, meaning Chinese submarines can launch nuclear weapons from littoral waters to hit U.S. targets. Don’t forget China’s H-6N bomber with its air-launched nuclear cruise missiles, and of course, China’s fractional orbital bombardment system, which in theory can put a nuclear hypersonic warhead into low Earth orbit. Then there is North Korea, which has developed its nuclear arsenal with help from both Russia and China. You can see why Trump wants to "discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world," which President Trump believes are very dangerous, White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said. RUSSIA’S QUIETER NUCLEAR SUBMARINES THREATEN NATO, FORMER COMMANDER WARNS Those dictators crave the optics. Maybe Trump can leverage the limelight. The trilateral summit won’t produce a treaty, but it might start a conversation. Here’s why. Over the past year, America’s geopolitical power has increased. The U.S.-China trade deficit is at its lowest level in 20 years. America is ahead in AI "superintelligence." Russia, on the other hand, is becoming an economic vassal state to China and a target of Ukraine’s long-range drone strikes on energy and military targets. In China, President Xi Jinping has carried out so many leadership purges that the powerful Central Military Commission is down to just two of its seven members. WE SHOULD USE REAGAN AS A GUIDE IN HANDLING OUR MODERN ARMS RACE WITH CHINA Despite the midterms, President Trump has momentum due in part to his military buildup. Don’t forget President Ronald Reagan notched big successes such as the 1987 Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces, or INF, Treaty, which eliminated an entire class of U.S. and Soviet nuclear weapons after control of Congress switched to the Democrats. And whatever Xi and Putin have to say in Shenzhen, America’s modernized triad remains the single most powerful bargaining chip for any future arms control. Here are the three key programs. TRUMP TURNS TO EMERGING TECH GIANT IN MULTI-BILLION BID TO RAMP UP US SUBMARINE PRODUCTION Sentinel nuclear missile. Look for the first test flight of the new Sentinel intercontinental ballistic missile, or ICBM, in 2027. The LGM-35 Sentinel missile will replace the 1970s-era Minuteman III missiles as the land-based missile leg of the triad. In wartime, ICBMs can hit targets about 30 minutes after launch. Sentinel completed a stacking test in September, with all missile components loaded into the cavernous launch silo at Vandenberg Space Force Base on the California coast. Over time, about 400 Sentinel missiles will be deployed in new silos across the missile fields of Montana, North Dakota and Wyoming. B-21 Raider stealth bomber. Today, a fleet of 76 B-52s and just 20 B-2 Spirit stealth bombers — of Midnight Hammer fame — comprises the air-delivered leg of the triad. The B-21 Raider is a sleek, gray stealth bomber that will join the triad soon. On Nov. 13, the B-21 completed its first weapons release on the test range, and plans call for accelerated production. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Columbia-class submarine. I saw the bow section of the 520-foot hull of the USS District of Columbia at the shipyard, and this new ballistic missile submarine is huge. The shipyards doubled their work output over the summer, bringing this lead submarine back on track for delivery in 2028, according to Rear Adm. Rob Gaucher, the U.S. Navy’s direct report program manager for undersea warfare. Eventually, 12 Columbia-class submarines will take over the sea-based mission of the nuclear deterrent and provide an assured second-strike capability by carrying 16 Trident II missiles apiece, each of which can be armed with up to 12 nuclear warheads. articles.title: A California mother started a therapy-dog programme after seeing firefighters struggle during wildfires; her nonprofit has since certified 500-plus dog teams and supported 150,000 first responders
articles.summary: Heidi Carman, a California mother and founder of First Responder Therapy Dogs in San Rafael, started her therapy dog programme after seeing how wildfires
articles.body: Heidi Carman, a California mother and founder of First Responder Therapy Dogs in San Rafael, started her therapy dog programme after seeing how wildfires weighed on the firefighters battling them. Alongside her certified therapy dog, Kerith, she founded the organisation to ease that emotional toll. By the end of 2025, her nonprofit organisation had certified more than 500 therapy dog teams and supported over 150,000 first responders. The therapy dog teams visit first responders across the country, offering relief from the chronic stress that comes with the job, and the work has drawn national recognition through the CNN Heroes programme.How California wildfires in 2020 led Heidi Carman and her therapy dog to comfort firefightersAccording to CNN, when massive wildfires hit California in 2020, Carman and her certified therapy dog made it their mission to comfort firefighters working on the front lines. SERVPRO, the cleanup and restoration company that sponsored the CNN Heroes broadcast, said the organisation has been certifying teams since 2021. By December 2025, it added, the organisation’s reach extended across 46 states.Why Heidi Carman’s studies in psychology and dog training shaped her goal for every first responderThe organisation’s own website describes Carman as its founder and executive director, and says her studies in psychology and dog training led her to create it. She is married, has five children, a grandson and a granddaughter, and has three therapy dogs of her own. Her ultimate goal, the site says, is to provide therapy dogs to every first responder in the United States.How former first responders and volunteer handlers help run the nonprofit from coast to coastThe organisation’s website lists a leadership team that mixes volunteer dog handlers with people who have worked in public safety. Lena Strickling and her dog, Birdie, were the second team to be certified. Tracy Ryan, now chief operating officer, joined in August 2021 with her dog, Sparkie, to bring therapy dog support to first responders on the East Coast.Michelle Detrick, a retired firefighter paramedic with 17 years of frontline experience, directs wildfire operations and community outreach. Separate outreach coordinators cover the Eastern and Western regions.How Heidi Carman became one of the Top 5 CNN Heroes of 2025 and what the honour brought her workAnderson Cooper revealed the Top 5 CNN Heroes of 2025, and Carman was among them. The honourees were celebrated at CNN Heroes: An All-Star Tribute, broadcast on 6 December and hosted by Cooper and fellow anchor Laura Coates, with viewers voting daily for the hero who inspired them most.Each of the Top 5 received $10,000 to further their work, SERVPRO reported. articles.title: Kim Jong Un's nuclear buildup sparks 'serious concern' ahead of Trump-Xi-Putin summit
articles.summary: IAEA chief Rafael Grossi warned Kim Jong Un's North Korean uranium enrichment expansion at Yongbyon is complete, calling it a serious concern.
articles.body: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un is accelerating his nuclear program, expanding a uranium enrichment facility that can produce plutonium for nuclear weapons, the United Nations' nuclear watchdog warned Wednesday, calling Pyongyang's growing program a "cause for serious concern." International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) Director General Rafael Grossi said the latest construction at the Yongbyon nuclear complex began in mid-September and was externally complete by late October, raising fresh alarms about North Korea's production of weapons-grade nuclear material. "The ongoing expansion of the DPRK's uranium enrichment programme remains a cause for serious concern," Grossi said in remarks to the IAEA's board of governors in Vienna, referring to North Korea by its official name, the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. TRUMP ARRIVES IN PHILIPPINES AHEAD OF XI JINPING SUMMIT IN CHINA AFTER GOP MIDTERM LOSSES The warning came as President Donald Trump prepared to meet President Xi Jinping and President Vladimir Putin on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, for an unprecedented three-way summit expected to address nuclear arms negotiations and other global security concerns. Trump had also floated the possibility of meeting Kim during his trip to China, potentially opening another diplomatic channel with the North Korean dictator as Pyongyang continues to reject demands that it abandon its nuclear arsenal. TRUMP CANNOT DETER XI AND PUTIN’S NUCLEAR GOALS WITH A STRATEGY DESIGNED FOR JUST ONE As he departed the White House on Monday, Trump told reporters that denuclearization would be among the issues discussed with world leaders. "We're going to talk about denuclearization – tough subject, because it's very hard for any of us to say we'll get rid of our nukes," Trump said. The president also raised the possibility of Kim joining the diplomatic discussions, although no meeting with the North Korean leader has been confirmed. "He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," Trump told reporters. Trump also said he believed there was an opportunity for progress. "So that'll be good. We have a chance to accomplish a lot," he added. TRUMP TEASES POTENTIAL KIM JONG UN MEETING LATER THIS YEAR The possibility of a meeting gained attention after Russia's Interfax news agency quoted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying Putin could meet Kim if the North Korean leader traveled to China for the summit, according to Reuters. Trump said Tuesday that Kim would like to meet with him, adding, "We'll see what happens." North Korea has repeatedly rejected calls to dismantle its nuclear weapons program, even as international monitors report continued construction and activity at key nuclear facilities. Grossi said the IAEA had previously reported ongoing enrichment operations at Yongbyon and Kangson, construction of an additional enrichment facility at Yongbyon and indications of further expansion of North Korea's production of weapons-grade nuclear material. "Since mid-September 2026, a further extension to the original Yongbyon enrichment facility has been under construction with the new extension externally complete by late-October 2026," Grossi said. The agency also observed indications that Yongbyon's 5-megawatt reactor, which can produce plutonium for nuclear weapons, likely will continue to operate in its seventh irradiation cycle. A separate light-water reactor at the complex resumed operations at the end of April following a shutdown, according to the agency. NORTH KOREA MISSILE COULD PUT GUAM IN RANGE AS KIM REBUFFS TRUMP OUTREACH: EXPERT "The continuation and further development of the DPRK's nuclear programme are clear violations of relevant UN Security Council resolutions and are deeply regrettable," Grossi said. The IAEA has not had inspectors inside North Korea since 2009, when Pyongyang expelled them. The agency now relies primarily on satellite imagery and other publicly available information to monitor nuclear developments, limiting its ability to independently verify activity inside the facilities. North Korea carried out its first nuclear weapons test in 2006 and five additional tests through 2017, prompting successive rounds of U.N. Security Council sanctions targeting its nuclear and ballistic missile programs. In September, IAEA member states also expressed "growing concern" over increased nuclear activity in North Korea, while Kim's sister, Kim Yo Jong, dismissed the pressure and said North Korea's status as a nuclear-armed country was "absolute" while calling those who continued to seek its denuclearization "idiots." TRUMP REVEALS EXACT NUMBER OF NORTH KOREA'S NUCLEAR WEAPONS Kim has also indicated that future talks with Washington would depend on the United States abandoning its demand for denuclearization and instead negotiating with North Korea as a nuclear-armed state. The two leaders met in Singapore in 2018, when they signed a broad statement committing to work toward the denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula. Their second summit, in Hanoi in 2019, ended without an agreement after negotiations broke down over North Korea's nuclear facilities and demands for sanctions relief. Trump and Kim met again in June 2019 at the Demilitarized Zone separating North and South Korea, where Trump briefly crossed into North Korean territory. articles.title: A woman suffered second-degree burns after hot barbecue sauce spilt on her thigh at a US restaurant; a jury ordered the chain to pay nearly $2.8 million
articles.summary: A jury in Bexar County, Texas, has ordered the San Antonio restaurant chain Bill Miller Bar-B-Q to pay $2.8 million in damages to a woman who suffered
articles.body: A jury in Bexar County, Texas, has ordered the San Antonio restaurant chain Bill Miller Bar-B-Q to pay $2.8 million in damages to a woman who suffered second-degree burns after spilling barbecue sauce on her thigh. Genesis Monita, now 19, was injured in May 2023 when the sauce, described in court as “dangerously hot”, spilt from its container. A jury of six men and six women unanimously found the injuries resulted from the company’s “gross negligence”. They awarded compensatory damages and almost $1.9 million in punitive damages.Why did a woman sue Bill Miller over hot barbecue sauceAccording to the San Antonio Express-News, Ms Monita and her sister went to the Bill Miller restaurant at Old Pearsall Road and Loop 410 on the morning of 19 May 2023 to buy breakfast tacos before school. After buying the food at the drive-thru, Ms Monita pulled into a nearby parking space to eat. She said the sauce was so hot that she dropped the container, spilling it onto her upper right thigh. According to the newspaper, the sauce went through her ripped jeans and left a burn.In her 2023 complaint, Ms Monita alleged that Bill Miller was negligent in giving her "dangerously hot" sauce, in not providing a container that was "adequate" to hold it, and in failing to warn her of the heat, the Express-News reported. The sauce she spilt was 189 degrees, according to the newspaper, which was above the 165 degrees set out in Bill Miller's policy. Mr McClenahan countered that 165 degrees is a minimum temperature needed to comply with safety rules and that the company has no policy prohibiting heating the sauce to 189 degrees, the Express-News said.Why did the jury award nearly $1.9 million in punitive damagesJurors deliberated for just under two hours on Friday before awarding Ms Monita $900,000 for past and future mental anguish, physical pain and impairment. They also awarded $25,225 for medical care expenses and $700 for lost earnings. The newspaper said the verdict included $25,000 for Ms Monita to have surgery to remove a scar left by the burn.After finding gross negligence, the jury had to decide on punitive damages on top of the compensatory award. The Express-News reported that jurors took about 15 minutes to award Ms Monita, who is 19, almost $1.9 million. During the punitive portion of closing arguments, her attorney, Lawrence Morales II, noted that Bill Miller had a net worth of nearly $83 million as of September, according to the newspaper. He first asked the jury to make the company pay 1% of that, almost $830,000, but after hearing Mr McClenahan's closing arguments, he asked for 10%, or about $8.3 million.Why did the jury award punitive damages against Bill MillerMr Morales told jurors a similar incident had occurred at the same restaurant in 2021, when a woman burned her abdomen after spilling barbecue sauce. He said Bill Miller did not change the way it does business after either incident. Of the award, he said, "It sends the message that companies cannot put profits over customer safety." Mr McClenahan, according to the newspaper, calculated that in the 865 days between the two incidents the company had dispensed more than 2.2 million ounces of barbecue sauce, giving out 2 ounces in a 4-ounce plastic cup. He said the company knew of no other instances of customers being burned.The company's history and the wider context. It said Bill Miller started a poultry and egg operation in 1950 and opened a fried chicken to-go restaurant in 1953, later adding hamburgers and barbecue. In 2022, the company announced a $55 million headquarters project on the West Side, which it said would allow it to increase its store count to about 150, according to the Express-News. The newspaper noted that the total award is similar to that in the 1992 McDonald's coffee case, in which Stella Liebeck, then 79, was awarded $160,000 in compensatory damages and $2.7 million in punitive damages. The case was ultimately settled out of court for less than $500,000.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Australian former music teacher caught sexually assaulting 12-year-old student on CCTV installed by his mother; abused him for over a year, gave birth to his baby, pleads guilty to 12 child abuse offences
articles.summary: A former music teacher in Australia has been sentenced to eight-and-a-half years in prison after pleading guilty to sexually abusing her 12-year-old
articles.body: A former music teacher in Australia has been sentenced to eight-and-a-half years in prison after pleading guilty to sexually abusing her 12-year-old student over a period of more than a year. The abuse came to light after the boy's mother installed security cameras at their home and discovered footage of the teacher assaulting her son.Naomi Takea Craig, 34, was sentenced on Tuesday, November 17, in the Western Australia District Court. According to reports by PerthNow, she will have to serve at least six years and six months before becoming eligible for parole. Craig pleaded guilty to 12 child abuse offences.CCTV cameras installed by mother exposed the abuseAccording to Australia's ABC, Craig was caught assaulting the boy in his living room after his mother installed CCTV cameras inside their home. The footage exposed the abuse, leading to Craig's arrest on the same day, just weeks before she was due to give birth.As revealed in court, Craig abused the child between August 2024 and December 2025, when he was aged 12 and 13. She gave birth to his baby in January 2026.According to The Australian, the victim's mother had previously trusted Craig to spend time alone with her son and had even allowed her to stay overnight at their home.How the former teacher groomed her studentCraig first met the boy after he moved to Mandurah in Western Australia, where she was working as a music teacher at Frederick Irwin Anglican School.Prosecutor Mark Nicol told the court that Craig exploited her position of authority to manipulate the child. According to The Australian, she sent him inappropriate photographs and videos of herself in swimwear and lingerie, along with explicit text messages. She also asked the boy to send her explicit images in return.During the sentencing proceedings, Nicol argued that the abuse was not an isolated incident but a repeated pattern of offending.“This was not a one-off impulsive decision — it was again and again and again,” he said, according to The Australian.The prosecutor also alleged that Craig knew the boy had experienced trauma and was neurodivergent, making him particularly vulnerable.“She knew he was a highly vulnerable child,” Nicol told the court.According to ABC, Craig wiped away tears when the prosecutor described the impact of her actions on the victim and his family as a “nightmare without end”.Judge says the child was legally incapable of consentingWhile handing down the sentence, Judge John Prior told Craig that the boy was legally incapable of consenting to the abuse.“You knew how old the child was when you were offending against him,” the judge said, according to ABC.He also addressed Craig's reported feelings towards the boy, highlighting the significant age difference and the child's vulnerability.“Everything before the court says you were in love with him, but there was a 20-year age gap and he was a vulnerable child at the time,” Prior said, as reported by The Australian.The court also heard that Craig had untreated bipolar disorder, ADHD and chronic hypomania when the offences took place. She had been receiving psychological and psychiatric assistance.Teacher banned from working with children againCraig's personal circumstances have also changed following the case. According to ABC, her husband, with whom she previously had a son, has separated from her, and a divorce is likely.In addition to her prison sentence, Craig has been placed on the sex offender register and made subject to a lifetime restraining order protecting the victim. She has also been permanently barred from working as a teacher.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Missouri labourer turned his 20-acre property into a landscape of hand-painted signs; decades later, more than 100 of his works found a home in museums
articles.summary: A stretch of land in Fulton, Missouri, gradually became covered with hand-painted messages, biblical references and pointed observations about American
articles.body: A stretch of land in Fulton, Missouri, gradually became covered with hand-painted messages, biblical references and pointed observations about American life. Its owner, Jesse Howard, was not a trained artist or someone who made his living through art. He earned money through manual work and odd jobs, spending much of his life in the small Missouri town. Yet, from the 1950s onwards, his property took on a very different character. Signs appeared across fences, buildings and the yard, each carrying words he wanted passers-by to read. Howard called the place Sorehead Hill. What began as a personal undertaking eventually attracted attention from art institutions far beyond his neighbourhood.The Missouri man behind the growing collectionHoward was born in 1885 in Shamrock, Missouri. He was one of ten children and had a twin sister. His early years included periods of travelling around the American West before he eventually settled in Fulton, where he spent most of his adult life.His working life was largely made up of practical jobs and physical labour. There was little in his background to suggest that his name would eventually become associated with an unusual body of American folk art. He did not follow a conventional artistic career. Instead, his creative output developed on the property where he lived.During the 1950s, Howard began placing painted objects around his roughly 20-acre site. Some featured biblical imagery, while others included model aeroplanes carrying patriotic messages. His displays attracted criticism from people living nearby, and his creations were repeatedly vandalised.How neighbourhood disputes shaped his growing collection of signsThe disagreements with neighbours became part of the story of the site. As objects disappeared or were damaged, Howard responded by producing more work. He also began making signs that communicated his frustrations and views about events around him.The messages covered several subjects. Biblical passages and religious interpretations appeared alongside references to local and national politicians. Some signs directly addressed people accused of stealing or damaging his creations. Howard's writing was often forceful, with statements extending across multiple lines.His approach to making the signs was distinctive. He used carefully arranged lettering, usually in black or red paint, against whitewashed wooden or metal surfaces. The capital letters were laid out in ruled lines, giving the boards a recognisable appearance. Some messages were lengthy enough to fill several lines, turning ordinary sections of the property into displays of his personal commentary.Over time, the signs spread across the fence, house, yard and surrounding outbuildings. The collection eventually numbered in the hundreds. Howard continued adding to it even as disagreements with neighbours persisted.The artist who brought Sorehead Hill to wider attentionAlthough the property was not universally welcomed by the surrounding community, Howard's work began attracting interest outside Fulton. A significant moment came in 1968, when artist Gregg Blasdel featured him in an essay titled The Grass-Roots Artist, published in Art in America.His signs subsequently appeared in exhibitions at the Walker Art Center in Minneapolis and the Philadelphia College of Art. The displays introduced his work to audiences who might otherwise never have encountered Sorehead Hill. The attention was a departure from the response Howard had received locally. His property had grown out of personal expression and neighbourhood disputes, but the objects were increasingly being considered as part of a wider American folk and outsider art tradition.How museums preserved Howard's signsIn the 1970s, the Kansas City Art Institute acquired a substantial collection of Howard's works. The institution later took responsibility for looking after the signs following his death in 1983.Preserving the collection became important because the objects had originally been made for an outdoor setting. They were part of a changing property, exposed to the elements and, at times, vandalism. Their removal into institutional collections allowed many examples of Howard's work to survive beyond the life of Sorehead Hill.A further transfer took place in 2016. The Kansas City Art Institute worked with Kohler Foundation, Inc., to move 187 objects from its collection to the John Michael Kohler Arts Center. The material included 80 signs, six sculptures and more than 50 archival documents. These objects were added to 12 Howard signs already held by the Arts Center.Two more signs entered the institution's collection in 2017, expanding its holdings of the Missouri artist's work.The lasting legacy of Howard's unconventional artHoward's signs were not created as a single exhibition or according to a planned artistic programme. They accumulated over several decades, reflecting the subjects that occupied his attention at different points in his life. Religion, patriotism, politics and disputes with people around him all found their way onto the boards.The property itself was central to how the work developed. Its fences and buildings provided space for the messages, while the repeated destruction and replacement of signs contributed to the site's constantly changing appearance.Sorehead Hill no longer exists in the same form as the landscape Howard created, but a substantial part of its visual record survives through museum collections. The objects now held by the John Michael Kohler Arts Center and other institutions offer a way to examine the work of a man who spent much of his life outside the recognised art establishment.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1960, architect Jules Gregory built a New Jersey home with a wave-shaped roof; after approval to sell a studio separately, buyers can now purchase the original house for $1.65 million or the studio for $995,000
articles.summary: A landmark piece of midcentury modern architecture in Lambertville, New Jersey, is back on the market with a new option for buyers.
articles.body: A landmark piece of midcentury modern architecture in Lambertville, New Jersey, is back on the market with a new option for buyers. Jules Gregory’s 1960 Wave House, known for its dramatic wave shaped roof, is now available separately from its detached studio after condo status was approved, according to Realtor.com and Sotheby’s International Realty.Buyers can purchase the original four bedroom home for $1.65 million, the 1,200 square foot studio for $995,000, or both properties together for $2.6 million. The change gives buyers flexibility while preserving the chance to own a rare example of Gregory’s architectural legacy.A home shaped by designThe Wave House was built in 1960 by architect Jules Gregory, whose work is known for blending modernist principles with organic forms. The home’s most recognisable feature is its wavy roofline, which rises and dips above the rooms below.Inside, the 1,700 square foot residence features curvy wood ceilings, exposed beams, stone details, glass walls, and oversized windows. The design creates a sense of movement, with spaces that expand and compress as you move through the home.The living area includes floor to ceiling windows that highlight the dramatic roofline. A sunken conversation lounge, beamed living room, and European inspired kitchen add to the home’s midcentury character.Why the listing changedEarlier this year, the Wave House and studio were offered together as a single package. That approach made sense for buyers interested in the full estate, but it limited options for those who wanted only one of the properties.The recent approval of condo status changed that. Now the two structures can be sold independently, giving buyers the choice to purchase the main home, the studio, or both.Listing agent Grant Wagner of Callaway Henderson Sotheby’s International Realty said the new arrangement makes the offering more flexible. He noted that a buyer who purchases both could later sell one of them separately.What the Wave House offersThe main home sits on approximately 6 acres and includes four bedrooms. Its open floor plan is designed to highlight the roofline and connect the interior with the surrounding landscape.The home’s glass walls and oversized windows frame views of the property, while the wood ceilings and exposed beams give the space warmth and texture. The result is a home that feels both sculptural and livable.Wagner said the Wave House will likely attract architecture enthusiasts who appreciate its dramatic roofline, expansive glass, and privacy. He also suggested that the property could appeal to buyers from New York, Philadelphia, or abroad who want to own a piece of architectural art.What the studio offersThe detached studio offers a different kind of living experience. It has a 1,200 square foot open floor plan, two en suite bedrooms, and newly updated bathrooms.The kitchen includes a waterfall island, a jewel box inspired accent wall, and concealed storage and appliances. The living room features a decorative fireplace and opens through double atrium doors to a bluestone patio overlooking a vegetable garden.The studio also includes new lighting, windows, HVAC, and other upgrades. Wagner described it as a sophisticated, turnkey space for someone seeking a weekend home or a minimalist lifestyle.A rare offering in LambertvilleThe two properties sit on a combined 10.03 acres, with the Wave House on about 6 acres and the studio on 4 acres. The setting offers privacy and proximity to the 70 mile Delaware and Raritan Canal State Park Trail for hiking and biking.The ability to purchase the properties separately adds a new layer of appeal. A buyer could own the main home as a primary residence and use the studio as a guest house, rental, or workspace.For architecture lovers, the Wave House represents a chance to own a piece of design history. For others, the studio offers a more accessible entry point into the estate. Either way, the listing gives buyers options that did not exist before.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: DNA showed a Washington man was the biological father of a child born in 2021, but a judge found the pregnancy resulted from sexual assault; an appeals court upheld the decision to deny him legal parenthood
articles.summary: DNA testing can establish biological relationships, but it does not automatically grant legal parental rights.
articles.body: DNA testing can establish biological relationships, but it does not automatically grant legal parental rights. In a Washington court case, a man sought legal recognition as the father of a child born in 2021, highlighting the distinction. The Washington Court of Appeals found the man couldn’t establish legal parentage, despite genetic testing showing a 99 percent or greater probability that he was the biological father, because the child was conceived through sexual assault. The November 16, 2026 decision illustrates how Washington’s parentage laws deal with pregnancies resulting from sexual violence, making the circumstances of conception central to the legal determination.Paternity dispute heard in courtAccording to the Washington Court of Appeals, the man, identified in the proceedings as A.D.-C., filed a petition in June 2024 seeking a formal determination that he is the parent of the child, identified as K.B.P.G. The child's mother, G.G.-A., opposed his request, saying the pregnancy was the result of sexual assault during their relationship. The couple met and started dating in 2019. They had a child in April 2021. Although the mother had listed another man on the child’s birth certificate, she did not dispute the biological connection established by the genetic testing.The Washington Court of Appeals held that the dispute was governed by the Washington Uniform Parentage Act, RCW 26.26A.465. The law permits a court to refuse legal parentage upon a showing by clear, cogent and convincing evidence that sexual assault resulted in conception.Competing narratives of the relationshipThe mother told the fact-finding hearing their relationship was one of constant sexual assault, intimidation and threats. She testified that the man threatened her and her older daughter, warning that he would involve immigration authorities or harm her family if she reported him. She also told of being followed by a vehicle, of repeated visits near her home and of alleged surveillance of her property. The woman didn't report the alleged assaults sooner because of fear, limited English proficiency and concerns over whether authorities would believe her, the Washington Court of Appeals said in an opinion released Wednesday. She supported her account with three witness statements, photographs of bruises on her arms, text messages and other evidence.The man had a different story of the events. He claimed their relationship was consensual, that they planned the pregnancy and that he had provided significant financial assistance to her business, home and childcare costs. But the Washington Court of Appeals noted there was no documentary evidence of the financial transfers he described. He also denied threatening anyone or sexually assaulting anyone.The evidence that led the lower court to its decisionA particularly important part of the proceedings dealt with an incident on June 23, 2020. The woman said the man broke into her apartment, tied her up and sexually assaulted her. The next day, she took photos of bruises on her arms that she said were caused by him.The trial court found her story credible and considered the photographs, the supporting declarations and testimony concerning other alleged incidents. It also heard evidence that her older daughter had called an aunt during a previous incident when she heard her mother crying.The Washington Court of Appeals said the trial court found the man’s explanations inconsistent and his testimony not credible. The child was conceived from the assault in June 2020, about 287 days before the child was born in April 2021, it said.Image Courtesy: Google GeminiYou use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Hunger Games to show Cardiff teen's artwork before film
articles.summary: Freja Brown beat more than 1,000 entries and met some of the stars after winning a competition.
articles.body:
A teenage Hunger Games fan has met the cast of the new film after her artwork won a competition, meaning it will be displayed at every cinema screening across the UK.

Freja Brown, 13, won the British Board of Film Classification's (BBFC) create the card competition, which ran ahead of the release of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping - the sixth film in the franchise.

Freja, from Cardiff, beat more than 1,000 entries from across the UK and said she was "so grateful" to be chosen.

Her design will be the official BBFC black card, which displays the age rating and classification details of the film before every cinema showing.

The Year nine student, whose favourite subject is art, only started oil painting three years ago.

Her mum Marie recalled the moment Freja found out about the competition while scrolling on social media.

"She just squealed and said, 'there's this competition where you can create a piece of art' and she loves making art. So, she was like, 'I'm gonna do it'."

"She's read all the books and watched all the movies, so being able to combine her love for the Hunger Games with her own art sounded really fun."

articles.title: Myanmar faces historic genocide verdict at UN court over Rohingya massacres
articles.summary: No state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.
articles.body:
When the judges of the International Court of Justice read out their verdict in the seven-year-old genocide case filed by The Gambia against Myanmar on Thursday, they could make history.

In the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948, after the Nazi Holocaust, dozens of individuals have been successfully prosecuted for the crime of genocide, in conflicts such as those in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.

But no state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.

"It would be a judgment of landmark importance if The Gambia were to win this case," says Arsalan Suleman, the lawyer leading the case against Myanmar at the court. "It would give renewed vitality to the 1948 Genocide Convention and to the notion of international legal accountability for crimes committed by a state."

The mass expulsion of the Rohingya population of Rakhine State in August and September 2017 was without question a military operation of exceptional brutality.

I was among a very small number of journalists who witnessed the deliberate burning of Rohingya villages in Rakhine, and also the dreadful human suffering of the hundreds of thousands who fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.

Their accounts of killing, torture and mass rape by Burmese soldiers have been thoroughly documented by human rights groups and a United Nations fact-finding mission .

I have on many occasions interviewed ethnic Rakhine people about their animosity towards the Muslim population, and I have documented the systematic obliteration of what remained of Rohingya villages by the Myanmar state.

But the question posed at the UN's top court, the ICJ, is whether all of this amounted to genocide.

The ICJ was established in 1945 to help settle disputes between states, not to try international crimes. However, it was chosen to address the attacks on Rohingyas in Myanmar because there were few other avenues of redress for the victims.

Myanmar authorities have denied accusations of ethnic cleansing or genocide, saying they were only responding to terrorist actions by Rohingya militants with so-called military "clearance operations".

A UN report in 2018 , based on hundreds of interviews, said the army's tactics were "grossly disproportionate to actual security threats". It said top military figures in Myanmar must be investigated for genocide in Rakhine State and crimes against humanity in other areas. Myanmar rejected the report.

As Myanmar was not a signatory to the International Criminal Court, it was not possible to file a case there against the officials accused of atrocities in Rakhine State.

Instead in November 2019 The Gambia, backed by the Organisation of Islamic Co-operation, filed a case at the ICJ, arguing that all states are bound by the Genocide Convention, so all have an interest in upholding it.

It accused the state in Myanmar, not just the military, of genocide.

This was a novelty in international law; a state not directly affected by an act, arguing that it had legal standing to make a complaint because it was indirectly affected by any violations of such an important convention.

Myanmar objected to this argument, but the ICJ judges ruled that The Gambia was eligible to file the case.

The case drew even more attention when the Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, who at the time headed the elected government in Myanmar, chose to lead the initial legal defence of her country at The Hague in person, for which she was widely criticised.

She had very limited influence over the actions of the Myanmar military in Rakhine State, but her refusal to condemn them dismayed many of those who until then had admired her courage and adherence to democratic principles.

Since she was deposed by a coup in 2021 and placed under arrest the defence has been led by a new team appointed by the military.

Historically, proving that genocide has been committed has been very difficult. Judges apply a high bar to this.

Typically, where there is no explicitly genocidal programme, like that of the Nazis, the judges require that the evidence presented at court must be such that the only reasonable inference from the actions of the defendants is that they had genocidal intent.

When Bosnia-Herzegovina filed a genocide case against Serbia at the ICJ in 1993, it took the court 14 years to conclude that while incidents like the 1995 massacre at Srebrenica did amount to genocide, there was not sufficient proof that the state of Serbia had genocidal intent, though it was found to have failed to prevent genocide.

Myanmar's lawyers and Aung San Suu Kyi have argued something similar.

Suu Kyi said that The Gambia's team mischaracterised a complex conflict and military operation, and that while she accepted that war crimes may have been committed against the Rohingyas, that is not proof of genocidal intent.

But Arsalan Suleman believes the weight of evidence his team gathered is enough to meet that high bar.

"What we presented to the court was the long history of discrimination targeting the Rohingya, and how that history, and the policies connected with it, provide a background to understand the government's language, rhetoric, propaganda, and policies that were part of the 2017 'clearance operations'," Suleman said.

"We discussed the 1982 citizenship law, and the tightening noose of discriminatory laws that restricted access to education, healthcare, livelihoods, and travel - all of which made life really impossible for the Rohingya and, we argued, was one of several indicators of genocidal intent."

What happens if the court does find in favour of The Gambia?

Myanmar would then find itself tarnished by having committed "the crime of crimes", as sitting on the same bench as Nazi Germany, the Rwandan Hutu militants and the Bosnian Serbs at Srebrenica.

That might seem a setback for Min Aung Hlaing, the general who now runs Myanmar, who above all was responsible for the military's operations in 2017, and who has been trying to improve his dismal international image in recent months.

There is no right of appeal against an ICJ verdict. However, there is also no penalty that follows an ICJ verdict.

The Burmese coup leader is focused mostly on rebuilding relations with neighbouring Asian countries, who are unlikely to pay too much attention to such a verdict, and much less on rebuilding relations with Western countries who do care.

But for the huge Rohingya diaspora this verdict matters a great deal.

"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of the Rakhine town of Buthidaung in 2017 and now lives in Canada.

"For the Rohingya, this trial is a moment of acknowledgement of our suffering after years of denial. The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades, not just this year."

He and other Rohingya activists hope that a ruling in favour of The Gambia will prompt more co-ordinated action by other countries to find a resolution which allows them to go home to Rakhine State, in safety.

More than a million are stuck in wretched camps in Bangladesh, barred from employment as international funding dries up.

But the obstacles to realising this hope are formidable.

Rakhine State has been ravaged by a conflict between the military and the insurgent Arakan Army, which now controls most of the territory. It is supported by the indigenous Rakhine population who are very hostile to the idea of the Rohingyas coming back.

Many Rohingya villages have been completely destroyed. And international support for them has faded over the years. Even an unprecedented genocide verdict at the world's highest court cannot change that reality.

articles.title: Idaho dropped 76 beavers from an aeroplane in parachute-equipped boxes in 1948 to move them into remote forests; the unusual experiment cost just $30 per four animals and helped establish new colonies
articles.summary: In 1948, Idaho’s Fish and Game Department used an unusual method to move 76 beavers into remote wilderness areas.
articles.body: In 1948, Idaho’s Fish and Game Department used an unusual method to move 76 beavers into remote wilderness areas. It dropped them from an aeroplane in boxes suspended beneath parachutes. The operation was intended to solve problems caused by transporting the animals through mountainous, heavily forested country with few roads.Earlier journeys involved trips on horses, mules and trucks, exposing beavers to heat, rough handling and delays. According to Elmo W. Heter’s paper, titled ‘Transplanting Beavers by Airplane and Parachute’, published in the Journal of Wildlife Management, the experiment provided a faster, cheaper, and safer transportation method. Observations made in late 1949 found that the relocated animals had built dams, constructed houses, and stored food.How did Idaho move beavers to remote release sitesIdaho had been moving beavers from places where they were plentiful and could damage irrigation systems, orchards, and other plantings. In the areas where they were released, the animals usually formed colonies, multiplied, and established fur-bearing populations.Heter also noted their contribution to improving habitats for game, fish and waterfowl, as well as watershed conservation. The department selected release sites through its conservation officers, working with the state fur supervisor and local Forest Service officials. The former transport system was difficult in Idaho’s mountains and remote forests. Beavers were first transported for several days on pack horses or mules before being loaded onto trucks. After reaching the nearest road to the selected site, they had to be carried again on pack animals. The long journeys exposed them to heat and rough handling, while they needed constant cooling and water.What made the beaver transport boxes suitable for parachute dropsParachutes were tested with dummy weights, and a 24-foot rayon parachute was chosen from surplus wartime stock. The parachute could carry 140 pounds, while a loaded box containing two beavers weighed between 80 and 105 pounds. The box measured 30 inches long, 16 inches wide, and 12 inches deep, and weighed about 20 pounds. It was made from surfaced lumber and had ventilation holes in its walls.Two sections fitted together like a suitcase. Rope lashings held the box shut during loading and flight, while elastic straps acted as spring hinges. When the parachute landed and its lines slackened, the straps pulled the box open, allowing the beavers to leave. The load kept the box securely closed during its descent.An old beaver helped test the aerial relocation methodBefore carrying out the operation, the team completed successful trials with dummy weights. The team then used an old male beaver named ‘Geronimo’ for repeated test drops at the flying field. After each landing, someone collected him as he scrambled from the box. Heter wrote that Geronimo eventually became resigned to the routine and would crawl back into his box when approached.The team later sent him into the hinterland with three young females. He remained in the box for some time after the females began inspecting their new surroundings. Heter reported that the colony was later well established. The aircraft used for the operation in Idaho was a Travelair, carrying the pilot, a conservation officer and eight crates of beavers.The relocated beavers built dams and stored food within a yearThe drops took place in autumn 1948. The team released 76 beavers, with one casualty. On the first drops, a light lashing broke before the parachute lines could hold the box closed. One beaver pushed its head through the opening, climbed onto the box, and fell when it was about 75 feet above the ground.Observations made late in 1949 showed that the transplanted beavers had built dams, constructed houses, and stored food. Heter estimated that moving four beavers cost about $30, including two boxes, two cargo parachutes and flying time.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Irish activist indicted in US over alleged destruction of $60M military plane
articles.summary: United States prosecutors say Daithi O'Corrain spent months planning the Shannon Airport attack that left a $60 million C-130H Hercules beyond repair
articles.body: An Irish anti-Israel activist was indicted in the United States after allegedly destroying a $60 million American military aircraft at an airport in Ireland, leaving the plane damaged beyond repair after what prosecutors described as months of meticulous planning. Federal prosecutors announced the indictment Tuesday, seven months after Daithi O'Corrain, 48, allegedly breached the security perimeter at Shannon Airport in western Ireland and broke into an unoccupied U.S. Air National Guard C-130H Hercules aircraft. Prosecutors said O'Corrain then spent hours damaging the aircraft, cutting critical wiring and hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit instruments, puncturing air ducts and pinching shut the aircraft's liquid oxygen line. 2 FOREIGN NATIONALS BREACH UK BASE HOUSING KEY US, NATO INTEL HUB AMID $556M EXPANSION The damage was so extensive it rendered the aircraft inoperable, and the $60 million plane will never return to active flight status, according to federal authorities. Photographs released by federal prosecutors show extensive damage inside the aircraft, including smashed cockpit instruments, severed wiring and damaged equipment. Other images show tools allegedly used in the attack and O'Corrain standing on the aircraft's roof before his arrest. Months of planning According to the indictment, O'Corrain spent months researching the aircraft's construction, acquiring tools and gallium, a metal capable of corroding aluminum, and using a flight-tracking app to monitor military aircraft. He also researched previous attacks on U.S. military planes at Shannon Airport and searched for locations where he could breach the airport's security perimeter. O'Corrain, who also goes by the name David Curran and is from County Cork in southern Ireland, was charged with destruction of government property, which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison. FBI Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle Jr. said the attack was meticulously planned and jeopardized critical military operations. "This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism. The defendant allegedly spent months researching the aircraft, acquiring tools and materials and preparing to maximize the destruction he could inflict," Barnacle said. "The FBI and our law enforcement partners will continue to pursue anyone who targets U.S. military assets, regardless of where those attacks occur." US EVACUATES 13 MILITARY AIRCRAFT FROM SECOND UK BASE AS NEW IRAN THREAT RAISES ALARM It remains unclear whether the United States has formally requested O'Corrain's extradition from Ireland. The Justice Department, Irish Department of Justice and Irish prosecutors did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment before publication. The C-130 Hercules is a four-engine turboprop military transport aircraft used to carry troops, equipment and supplies, including into remote areas with short, rough runways. First introduced in the 1950s, it remains in service today, while the C-130H variant involved in the Shannon Airport incident dates to the 1970s. The aircraft was parked on a taxiway and was due to depart for another country on a U.S. military assignment, according to the indictment. The indictment outlined how the alleged attack unfolded. O'Corrain allegedly breached Shannon Airport's security perimeter at approximately 4:40 a.m. on April 11 before crossing the airfield and breaking through the aircraft's rear crew door. Once inside, he barricaded himself using tools and supplies he had brought with him. He also covered the aircraft's windows with the flight crew's hammocks, except for the cockpit windows, prosecutors said. Prosecutors said he demonstrated detailed knowledge of the aircraft's critical components and how to destroy them while protecting himself. They warned that the aircraft could have been rocked by a massive explosion had O'Corrain cut through its liquid oxygen line instead of pinching it shut. Five hours later, the flight crew returned to prepare for departure and spotted O'Corrain through a cockpit window, prompting them to alert airport security. O'Corrain allegedly climbed through a roof hatch and continued damaging the aircraft, striking its exterior with an axe and pouring unidentified substances and placing objects, including ball bearings, into its fuel tanks. Video circulating online at the time appeared to show a man in dark clothing walking along the wing of the aircraft near the engines and fuselage. Irish police arrived shortly afterward and arrested him. "These charges send a clear and powerful message that attacks on U.S. military assets — and thus our national security — will not be tolerated," U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said. Criminal charges in Ireland O'Corrain is also facing criminal charges in Ireland over the same incident. He was initially denied bail before securing his release through the Irish High Court, according to RTÉ. Irish prosecutors have since moved to bring the case to trial, with O'Corrain facing charges, including criminal damage to the aircraft and interference with airport operations. He is scheduled to appear in court again in January. O'Corrain has drawn support from pro-Palestinian activists in Ireland. An online fundraiser describes him as an independent peace activist and portrays the incident as an act of resistance against the U.S. military's presence in Ireland and American support for Israel. The campaign features a raised fist gripping a hammer — imagery associated with labor and revolutionary movements — superimposed over a photograph of the aircraft. "An inspiring act of direct action was carried out at Shannon Airport to resist the unwanted presence of the US Military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel’s genocide," organizer Tracey Ryan wrote. History of airport breaches Shannon Airport, which has long served as a transit hub for U.S. military aircraft, was also used by President Donald Trump and Air Force One during his visit to Ireland in September. The alleged attack followed three other security breaches at Shannon Airport in 2025, according to the indictment. In May, three people were arrested after driving a van through the airport's perimeter fence. Weeks later, three others breached the airfield and sprayed a U.S. military aircraft with paint, temporarily grounding it. Unlike those earlier incidents, the April attack allegedly resulted in the permanent loss of a U.S. military aircraft, with O'Corrain now facing prosecution in two countries.
